speaker: Pieter van der Does
title: Adyen success story: Pieter van der Does building one of Europe’s largest fintech unicorns
question: In global B2B payments, how do providers realistically sequence expansion into demanding Asian markets like Japan?
guest: For example, we announced that we are with Microsoft in Japan, our latest geographical expansion. How that works is you have merchants like that who say, 'We also want to use you in our next market,' so we follow the client. But if you look at Japan, that took three years of technical preparation before we could launch there. It's a market where you launch when you have things ready—it's not a 'launch fast and iterate' market. You want to make sure you have a great quality of product, and even then we start with an international merchant in that market who has the benefit of working with us across multiple markets, and therefore has a bias to choose an international player rather than connect to multiple local vendors, which would be very difficult. So it's talking to our merchants and comparing which market they are expanding into next that designs our roadmap. Sometimes that's with a physical presence and sometimes without—we connect a country's payment methods and get licenses there without necessarily having an office.

points.core: Providers follow existing multinational clients into new countries rather than entering cold.
points.note: Accept: anchoring new-country entry on current global customers expanding there, letting merchant demand dictate the geographic roadmap. Do not credit: generic advice to do market research or hire local sales reps first.

points.core: Global merchants prefer one unified provider over integrating separate local payment vendors.
points.note: Accept: international enterprises have a structural bias toward consolidating multiple regions on a single cross-border platform to avoid multi-vendor integration complexity. Do not credit: vague mentions of customer loyalty or brand trust.

points.core: Demanding markets like Japan reject rapid iteration in favor of upfront completeness.
points.note: Accept: markets like Japan require multi-year technical preparation and full product maturity at launch rather than shipping an MVP and iterating. Do not credit: generic claims that Japan has cultural differences or strict regulations without noting the anti-MVP launch bar.

points.core: Market entry requires local payment rails rather than mandatory physical offices.
points.note: Accept: obtaining local licenses and connecting local payment methods often suffices to serve a country without opening a local branch office. Do not credit: claiming physical offices are always required or never useful.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Providers typically enter Japan late and in stages, not as a first Asian market. The usual sequence starts with lighter-touch hubs, usually Singapore and Hong Kong, sometimes Australia, where licensing is faster, English-language regulation is accessible, and regional treasury flows concentrate. These build the compliance track record and corridor volume that later support a Japan case.

Japan itself usually begins through partnership rather than a licence: serving Japanese flows cross-border, or riding on a local bank or licensed partner for yen collection and payout via the Zengin domestic clearing system. This tests demand without the full regulatory burden.

Only once volumes justify it do providers pursue their own registration, typically as a Funds Transfer Service Provider under the Payment Services Act. This requires a local entity, resident management, Japanese-language compliance and operations, and patient engagement with the FSA and local finance bureau, often taking a year or more. Some shortcut this by acquiring a licensed local firm.

After licensing, direct clearing access and localised product follow: invoice-based bank transfer workflows, local reconciliation conventions, and Japanese-language support. Wise, Airwallex and Payoneer broadly followed this pattern.

points.why: The response bases market sequencing on regional hubs and corridor volume without tying entry to existing multinational clients expanding into Japan.
The response gives no account of why global merchants prefer one cross-border provider to integrating separate local vendors.
The response describes testing demand through partners and localizing later, so it misses Japan’s requirement for a mature product at launch.
The response mentions licensing and domestic clearing without explaining that providers can connect local payment methods and obtain the necessary licenses without opening an office.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Global B2B payment providers rarely enter Japan directly; instead, they sequence expansion from regional hubs to phased local licensing. Most first anchor APAC operations in Singapore or Hong Kong, using predictable regulatory regimes to build regional FX liquidity, treasury, and compliance teams. They then enter Japan through domestic bank or licensed partnerships, initially terminating cross-border JPY payouts for existing overseas clients via local banks connected to the Zengin clearing network. This validates corridor volume before committing to multi-year licensing.

Once demand justifies onshore investment, providers incorporate locally and pursue tiered registration with Japan’s Financial Services Agency. Firms typically obtain a Type 2 Funds Transfer Service Provider license first, accepting its ¥1 million per-transaction cap to onboard smaller SMB and marketplace flows while proving strict funds safeguarding and Japanese-language compliance. Only in the final stage do mature providers secure a Type 1 license to lift transfer caps for enterprise trade, pursue direct Zengin connectivity, and localize domestic workflows like virtual *furikomi* collection accounts.

points.why: The response uses payouts for existing overseas clients to validate corridor volume but never says those clients’ own expansion drives the choice to enter Japan.
The response never explains that multinational merchants prefer a single provider to avoid integrating separate local vendors.
The response proposes launching limited payout services first and expanding in stages, with multi-year licensing discussed after initial demand validation.

The response describes access to local payment rails through bank partners and later local incorporation but never establishes that local licensing and payment connectivity can suffice without a physical office.

noweb.answer:
Global B2B payment providers rarely enter demanding Asian markets like Japan with a full domestic buildout; instead, they sequence expansion to validate volume before absorbing heavy regulatory and integration costs. Providers typically anchor regional operations in Singapore or Hong Kong first, serving Japan remotely by routing cross-border flows for existing multinational clients through correspondent banks or licensed local aggregators.

Once corridor volume justifies deeper commitment, providers establish a local entity and pursue Financial Services Agency licensing, navigating the ¥1 million per-transfer cap on Type II Funds Transfer Service Providers via compliant commercial-agency models or the stringent Type I license required for high-value B2B settlements. Concurrently, they partner with Japanese banks to access the Zengin clearing network and issue virtual accounts for *furikomi* transfers. Only with domestic rails live do they target native Japanese enterprises, localizing KYB onboarding, tax-invoice workflows, and ERP integrations while partnering with domestic banks, trading houses, and accounting platforms to earn institutional trust.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Providers usually expand into Japan in stages. They start from a regional hub such as Singapore or Hong Kong, where licensing is quicker and corridors are already established. From there they serve Japanese counterparties cross-border, mostly for inbound collections and payouts to Japanese suppliers. Local bank partners handle yen settlement and access to Zengin, Japan's domestic clearing network. This lets them test demand without carrying Japan's compliance costs.

Once volume justifies it, they set up a local entity and register as a funds transfer service provider under Japan's Payment Services Act. That registration requires strong AML controls and safeguarding of customer funds, and the regulators move slowly. The Type I licence, needed for large transfers, is harder still.

Commercial localization follows. That means Japanese-language support and documentation, compatibility with Japan's Qualified Invoice System, and integrations with local accounting tools such as freee and Money Forward. Japanese buyers often expect payment on bank transfer or bill terms rather than cards, so providers build for that. Relationships with banks, trading companies and system integrators count for a lot.

Most players move from partnerships to licences to full local products over several years. Japan's conservative procurement culture rewards patience and credibility more than speed.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Global B2B payment providers typically enter demanding Asian markets like Japan in deliberate phases rather than building direct infrastructure on day one. They usually begin with a partner-led model, routing cross-border payouts and collections for existing global clients through local sponsor banks or licensed domestic intermediaries. This validates corridor volume and local workflows without multi-year regulatory delays.

Once volume justifies deeper investment, providers incorporate a local entity, hire domestic compliance and country leadership, and localize onboarding, support, and invoicing workflows. On the regulatory side, they often pursue an initial license—such as Japan’s Type 2 Funds Transfer Service Provider registration, capped at one million yen per transfer—or acquire a locally licensed firm to build a compliance track record with the Financial Services Agency.

Only after demonstrating operational rigor do providers seek high-value authorizations, like Japan’s Type 1 license for uncapped transfers, and direct access to domestic clearing rails such as the Zengin System to cut costs and win domestic enterprise volume.

noweb.answer: Providers typically sequence expansion into demanding Asian markets like Japan by moving gradually from light-touch cross-border coverage to full local infrastructure. They usually begin by serving existing multinational clients' inbound flows through local banking partners or licensed aggregators, which validates demand and builds market familiarity without triggering immediate licensing delays. In parallel, they establish a local legal entity, hire experienced compliance and relationship leaders, and begin the lengthy regulatory process—such as securing a Funds Transfer Service Provider registration with Japan's Financial Services Agency—while adapting products to local norms like domestic bank transfers, local-currency settlement, and invoicing or tax-compliance rules. Once direct access to domestic clearing rails like Zengin is secured through Tier-1 bank partnerships or direct licensing, providers can improve margins, settlement speed, and reconciliation accuracy. Only after proving reliability, security, and local-language support do they realistically scale into outbound cross-border and domestic enterprise sales, often co-selling alongside trusted local banks or system integrators to overcome corporate risk aversion.

They can often offer that service through a licensed local partner while they learn how much volume is repeatable and what it costs to handle FX, compliance, reconciliation, and support.

noweb.answer:
Providers typically start with a narrow payment corridor where existing customers already have demand, such as paying Japanese suppliers in yen. They often work with a local bank or licensed payments partner to reach domestic payment rails while they establish which activities they can perform under that arrangement and which require their own authorization.

A limited launch lets them test what matters to finance teams in practice: settlement times, FX pricing, beneficiary details, reconciliation, and how quickly someone can resolve a failed payment in Japanese. They expand once they see repeat volume and can support it reliably. That might mean adding local collections, more corridors, or direct integrations. A local entity or their own license can make sense when regulation requires it or when volume and margins justify the cost. The sequence depends more on customer demand, regulatory obligations, and operating economics than on a fixed country-by-country rollout.

models.answer:
Providers usually start with one payment corridor and one customer need. For Japan, that might mean helping existing overseas clients pay Japanese suppliers in yen. A licensed local bank or payment partner can handle domestic payouts while the provider learns what it takes to get funds to suppliers on time and reconcile each invoice. That gives the provider evidence of repeat demand before it commits to a broader launch.

Offering Japanese businesses the ability to collect funds or send money abroad is a separate expansion decision. Before launch, the provider needs to establish which activities its own permissions or a partner’s license cover and put the required controls in place. It can then add Japanese-language onboarding and support, local bank integrations, and more corridors as customers need them. If sustained volume justifies the fixed costs and greater control, the provider may pursue its own license or direct bank relationships. A partner-led model can also be the long-term choice.

points.why: The candidate describes serving existing clients’ cross-border payout needs without tying market selection to those clients’ own geographic expansion.
The candidate gives no reason why multinational merchants would consolidate payments with one provider to avoid integrating multiple local vendors.
The candidate proposes learning from a limited corridor before broadening the launch and gives no Japan-specific requirement for upfront technical maturity.
The candidate says a licensed local partner can handle payouts but leaves open whether the provider itself needs a local office.
